topics: 🦌 'Like the Gazelle and the Deer' — Rabbi Akiva's source for feeding a blemished firstborn to a gentile
🩸 Feeding It to a Menstruating Woman — Beit Shammai forbid, Beit Hillel permit
🐄 Skinning 'From the Feet' — why this method is barred for a firstborn and other disqualified offerings
🩹 Bloodletting on a Firstborn — may one save it even by causing a permanent blemish?
🍯 The Barrel of Teruma Parallel — Rabbi Elazar links the bloodletting dispute to a case of doubtful impurity
🔗 Testing the Parallel — the Gemara probes whether the two disputes really match

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Feeding, Skinning, and Saving a Blemished Firstborn
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 33a–33b
overview.hebrewSource: בְּכוֹר שֶׁאֲחָזוֹ דָּם, אֲפִילּוּ מֵת — אֵין מַקִּיזִין לוֹ דָּם, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara continues analyzing Beit Hillel's ruling that non-priests, and even gentiles, may share a blemished firstborn — tracing Rabbi Akiva's source to the phrase 'like the gazelle and the deer,' and extending the discussion to whether a menstruating woman may eat it. A related baraita then bars skinning a firstborn or other disqualified consecrated animal 'from the feet,' a technique that keeps the hide intact but is judged undignified for sacred meat. The daf's new mishna asks a sharper question: if a firstborn becomes dangerously congested with blood, may one let its blood to save it, even though the incision itself may cause a permanent blemish? Rabbi Yehuda, the Rabbis, and Rabbi Shimon each draw the line differently, and the Gemara compares their dispute to an unrelated case of doubtfully-impure teruma.

slides.title: 🦌 Why Rabbi Akiva Includes the Gentile
slides.subtitle: Deuteronomy 15:22 compares disqualified sacrifices to undomesticated game

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: What is Rabbi Akiva's reason for saying even a gentile may eat a blemished firstborn?

lines.speaker: Rabbi Akiva
lines.text: The verse says כַּצְּבִי וְכָאַיָּל — 'like the gazelle and like the deer.' Just as a gentile may eat a gazelle or deer, he may eat a disqualified consecrated animal.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But the phrase 'gazelle and deer' appears three times regarding disqualified offerings (12:15, 12:22, 15:22) — what do the other two teach?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: One teaches Rabbi Yitzḥak and Rabbi Oshaya's rulings; the third teaches that just as a gazelle and deer are exempt from having their firstborn count as bekhor, so too disqualified consecrated animals are exempt from that status.

callout.label: Underlying logic:
callout.text: Once an animal is disqualified from the altar, the Torah repeatedly likens it to ordinary wild game — open to anyone, priest or not, Jew or gentile.

slides.title: 🩸 May a Menstruating Woman Eat the Blemished Firstborn?
slides.subtitle: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argue from the same 'breast and thigh' comparison as before

nodes.content: ❓ Beit Shammai forbid feeding it to a niddah; Beit Hillel permit
📜 Beit Shammai: 'their flesh shall be yours' (Num. 18:18) likened to the priestly breast/thigh, which a niddah may not eat
✅ Beit Hillel: that verse is only about an unblemished firstborn; for the blemished one, 'the impure and pure alike may eat it' (Deut. 15:22)

🔀 Beit Shammai's limit: that leniency covers only impurity from an outside source (e.g. a corpse), not impurity from the body itself, like a niddah — proven from the Paschal offering, where only 'impure through a corpse' is included
↩️ Beit Hillel reply: the Paschal verse specifies 'impure through a corpse'; here the Torah writes 'impure' with no qualifier — no distinction applies

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: Beit Hillel's plain reading of the unqualified word 'impure' wins out — every type of impurity is included.

slides.title: 🐄 Skinning a Firstborn 'From the Feet'
slides.subtitle: A baraita bans this hide-preserving technique — but why, and according to whom?
rows: May not skin from the feet
It is unnecessary extra effort not needed for the Festival
May not skin from the feet, even on a weekday, even if blemished
Rav Ḥisda: follows Beit Shammai — a blemished firstborn keeps its sanctity, so it must be handled as sacrificial meat
May not skin from the feet
Rav Ḥisda: follows Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, who holds their sanctity survives slaughter

callout.label: Other reasons offered:
callout.text: Rav Mari: the gain to the hide is offset by damage to the meat. Ravina (in the West): it looks like performing sacrificial labor. Rabbi Yosei bar Avin: a decree lest people raise flocks while waiting to sell the hides.

slides.title: 🩹 New Mishna: Bloodletting to Save a Congested Firstborn
slides.hebrewSource: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: יַקִּיז, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה בּוֹ מוּם... רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: יַקִּיז, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה בּוֹ מוּם
slides.label: Three positions:
slides.text: Rabbi Yehuda: even if the firstborn will die, one may never let its blood, since the incision might cause a blemish. The Rabbis: one may let blood only in a spot that will not cause a permanent blemish; if it does cause one, the animal may not later be slaughtered on the strength of that particular blemish. Rabbi Shimon: one may let blood even where it will cause a blemish, and the animal may then be slaughtered on that very blemish.

slides.title: 🔗 Rabbi Elazar's Parallel to the Barrel of Teruma
slides.subtitle: The Gemara maps the bloodletting dispute onto an unrelated mishna about doubtfully-impure oil — then tests the fit

steps.content: 1️⃣ Terumot mishna: a barrel of teruma with doubtful impurity — Rabbi Eliezer says safeguard it; Rabbi Yehoshua says no need; Rabban Gamliel says leave it untouched

2️⃣ Proposed match: Rabbi Meir (blood only where no blemish results) ~ Rabbi Eliezer; the Rabbis (blood even where it causes a blemish) ~ Rabbi Yehoshua; Rabbi Yehuda (never let blood) ~ Rabban Gamliel
3️⃣ Gemara objects, repeatedly: each sage might rule differently here versus there — direct action versus indirect cause, certain death versus possible salvation (Elijah may yet purify the barrel)

4️⃣ Final answer: the two disputes rest on entirely different verses, so no firm parallel can be drawn at all — though 'all agree' on separate points, e.g. that repeated leavening of a meal offering or repeated castration each carries its own liability

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: A tempting structural parallel between two unrelated disputes can still fail once each sage's true reasoning is examined case by case.

summary.principle: Once disqualified from the altar, a firstborn is treated like ordinary game — open even to gentiles and, per Beit Hillel, to a niddah — yet its carcass must still be skinned with dignity, and the Sages sharply debate how far one may go to save a living firstborn from illness.

flowSteps.content: 🦌 Rabbi Akiva: 'like the gazelle and deer' permits even a gentile to eat a blemished firstborn
🩸 Beit Hillel: the unqualified word 'impure' in Deut. 15:22 includes a niddah, against Beit Shammai's distinction
🐄 Baraita bars skinning 'from the feet' — for a firstborn per Beit Shammai, for other disqualified animals per R' Elazar b'R' Shimon

columns.content: 🩹 R' Yehuda: never let blood, even to save the animal's life
🩹 Rabbis/R' Shimon: may let blood, with or without limits on the resulting blemish

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: sanctity of a disqualified firstborn constrains how it is handled long after it stops being fit for the altar

quiz.q: What verse does Rabbi Akiva use to permit even a gentile to eat a blemished firstborn?
o: "You shall not redeem" (Numbers 18:17)
"Like the gazelle and like the deer" (Deuteronomy 15:22)
"The impure and the pure may eat it alike" (Deuteronomy 15:22)
"It shall not be redeemed" (Leviticus 27:33)
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva reasons that just as a gentile may eat a gazelle or deer, he may eat a disqualified consecrated animal, since the verse compares them.

quiz.q: How does Beit Hillel justify permitting a menstruating woman (niddah) to eat a blemished firstborn?
o: They forbid it just like Beit Shammai
The Torah writes 'impure' without qualification in Deuteronomy 15:22, unlike the Paschal offering where 'impure through a corpse' is specified
Only priests may eat it, so the question is irrelevant
It applies only to unblemished firstborns
quiz.e: Beit Hillel note that the unqualified term 'impure' includes all forms of impurity, unlike the Paschal offering's law which specifically names impurity from a corpse.

quiz.q: According to Rav Ḥisda, whose opinion underlies the baraita's ban on skinning a firstborn 'from the feet'?
o: Rabbi Akiva's
Beit Shammai's, who hold a blemished firstborn retains sacrificial sanctity
Beit Hillel's
Rabban Gamliel's
quiz.e: Rav Ḥisda attributes the ban to Beit Shammai, who hold that a blemished firstborn must still be treated as sacrificial meat, making the feet-skinning technique inappropriate.

quiz.q: In the new mishna, what does Rabbi Yehuda rule about letting the blood of a firstborn congested with excess blood?
o: One may always let blood freely
One may never let its blood, even if the animal will die, because the incision might cause a blemish
One may let blood only on a Festival
One must let blood only in a place that will not blemish it
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda takes the strictest position: bloodletting is forbidden entirely, even at the cost of the animal's life, since it risks causing a blemish.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara ultimately question the parallel Rabbi Elazar draws between the bloodletting dispute and the barrel-of-teruma dispute?
o: Because the two disputes are recorded by different tannaim entirely

Because each sage's position in one case might differ in the other, due to differences like direct versus indirect action or certain versus possible loss, and the two disputes rest on different verses
Because the barrel of teruma has nothing to do with impurity
Because Rabbi Elazar later retracted the comparison
quiz.e: The Gemara repeatedly shows that a sage's ruling in one case need not carry over to the other case, since the underlying considerations (direct action vs. indirect cause, certain death vs. possible rescue) differ, and concludes the disputes stem from different verses.
